title: One-Way Relay: Two Kinases to a Smad

scenes.visual: Dark navy canvas. Across the upper half runs a schematic cell membrane cross-section (labelled 'Schematic' in a small corner tag) with warm cytosol below and a softly glowing golden nuclear rim at lower right. Two cyan Type II receptor blocks glow steadily on the membrane while two indigo Type I receptor blocks sit apart with slate-grey FKBP12 caps locked over their inner flaps. Crisp white title fades in and out across the upper band: 'One-Way Relay: Two Kinases to a Smad'. Ambient drift keeps cytosol particles moving slowly.

scenes.tts: An active kinase sits in your cell membrane all day, yet the cell stays quiet. What holds it back until TGF beta arrives, and how does the message reach DNA so fast?
scenes.caption: An active kinase sits in your cell membrane all day, yet the cell stays quiet. What holds it back until TGF-β arrives, and how does the message reach DNA so fast?
scenes.visual: Carried membrane cross-section from s00. Camera holds wide as cyan Type II receptors pulse softly with a 'Type II (active)' label, while indigo Type I receptors drift slowly out of reach, sealed by folded GS flaps and slate FKBP12 caps ('Type I (locked)'). A faint dashed arrow points from the membrane straight down to the glowing nuclear rim ('DNA').
scenes.narration: An active kinase sits in your cell membrane all day, yet the cell stays quiet. What holds it back until TGF-β arrives, and how does the message reach DNA so fast?

scenes.tts: Many growth factor relays chain several enzymes inside the cell before any gene responds. Transforming growth factor beta takes a shortcut. Its receptors are serine and threonine kinases of two types. Type two stays active all the time, like a lit match waiting in the membrane.
scenes.caption: Many growth factor relays chain several enzymes inside the cell before any gene responds. Transforming growth factor β takes a shortcut. Its receptors are serine/threonine kinases of two types. Type II stays active all the time, like a lit match waiting in the membrane.
scenes.visual: Carried membrane view. A faint schematic ghost of a multi-step cascade fades away on the left so the screen clears to the single membrane. Spotlight warms the two cyan Type II kinase domains inside the cytosol; a gentle ember shimmer orbits their active sites ('Always active'). Type I remains apart in cool indigo, showing its folded GS flap ('GS domain') capped by slate FKBP12 ('FKBP12 lock').
scenes.narration: Many growth factor relays chain several enzymes inside the cell before any gene responds. Transforming growth factor β takes a shortcut. Its receptors are serine/threonine kinases of two types. Type II stays active all the time, like a lit match waiting in the membrane.

scenes.tts: At rest, type one cannot fire on its own. A short inner stretch called the GS domain folds shut, capped by a small safety catch called FKBP twelve. Now an amber TGF beta dimer arrives from outside the cell. It binds two cyan type two chains first, then pulls two indigo type one chains into a four-receptor complex.
scenes.caption: At rest, type I cannot fire on its own. A short inner stretch called the GS domain folds shut, capped by a small safety catch called FKBP12. Now an amber TGF-β dimer arrives from outside the cell. It binds two cyan type II chains first, then pulls two indigo type I chains into a four-receptor complex.
scenes.visual: Carried membrane view. Zoom gently onto the upper membrane. An amber linked two-lobe block ('TGF-β dimer', schematic) descends from the extracellular space and docks between two cyan Type II outer domains. Immediately, two indigo Type I receptors slide laterally through the bilayer to contact both the amber dimer and the cyan Type II chains, forming a compact four-receptor cluster. Empathy fix: Label 'GS domain (regulatory stretch)'.
scenes.narration: At rest, type I cannot fire on its own. A short inner stretch called the GS domain folds shut, capped by a small safety catch called FKBP12. Now an amber TGF-β dimer arrives from outside the cell. It binds two cyan type II chains first, then pulls two indigo type I chains into a four-receptor complex.

scenes.tts: Pause and predict. Suppose a mutation breaks the type two kinase so it cannot transfer phosphate, while type one stays normal. When TGF beta arrives, will the receptors still assemble, and will type one get phosphorylated?
scenes.caption: Pause and predict. Suppose a mutation breaks the type II kinase so it cannot transfer phosphate, while type I stays normal. When TGF-β arrives, will the receptors still assemble, and will type I get phosphorylated?
scenes.visual: Carried four-receptor complex shifts slightly left and dims to 70% brightness; cyan Type II's inner kinase glow switches off and gets an amber ring label 'Kinase-dead Type II'. A high-contrast question card enters on the right: 'Type II kinase dead: Do receptors assemble? Is Type I phosphorylated?'
scenes.narration: Pause and predict. Suppose a mutation breaks the type II kinase so it cannot transfer phosphate, while type I stays normal. When TGF-β arrives, will the receptors still assemble, and will type I get phosphorylated?

scenes.visual: Question card remains steady and legible on the right while a subtle progress arc sweeps slowly around the card edge. On the left, the amber TGF-β dimer hovers just above the muted cyan and indigo receptors with gentle ambient drift so the frame stays alive during thinking time.

scenes.tts: The four chains still assemble outside, because ligand binding happens on the outer domains. Inside, nothing happens, because type one cannot light itself. Restore the type two kinase, and bright yellow phosphates jump onto the GS domain. FKBP twelve pops off, and the type one kinase opens active.
scenes.caption: The four chains still assemble outside, because ligand binding happens on the outer domains. Inside, nothing happens, because type I cannot light itself. Restore the type II kinase, and bright yellow phosphates jump onto the GS domain. FKBP12 pops off, and the type I kinase opens active.
scenes.visual: Question card clears. Left side shows the four chains snapping together around amber TGF-β while the dimmed Type II inner lobe stays dark and indigo Type I remains locked. Then Type II's cyan glow switches back on: bright yellow phosphate discs ('P') arc from Type II onto Type I's GS domain. The slate FKBP12 cap detaches and drifts away; the GS flap swings open, lighting the indigo Type I kinase bright.
scenes.narration: The four chains still assemble outside, because ligand binding happens on the outer domains. Inside, nothing happens, because type I cannot light itself. Restore the type II kinase, and bright yellow phosphates jump onto the GS domain. FKBP12 pops off, and the type I kinase opens active.

scenes.tts: That phosphorylated GS stretch now docks the next protein in line, a Smad. Remarkably, a Smad is itself a transcription factor. Active type one adds two phosphates to serines at the end of the Smad tail. The receptor just signalled straight to a DNA-binding protein.
scenes.caption: That phosphorylated GS stretch now docks the next protein in line, a Smad. Remarkably, a Smad is itself a transcription factor. Active type I adds two phosphates to serines at the end of the Smad tail. The receptor just signalled straight to a DNA-binding protein.
scenes.visual: Carried active receptor complex at top. An emerald green block ('R-Smad', showing two labelled lobes: 'MH1' and 'MH2' with a short tail) glides up from the cytosol and docks onto the phosphorylated GS stretch of indigo Type I. Two bright yellow phosphate discs snap onto the tip of the emerald tail. Label appears cleanly beside the cascade: 'Type II → Type I → R-Smad'.
scenes.narration: That phosphorylated GS stretch now docks the next protein in line, a Smad. Remarkably, a Smad is itself a transcription factor. Active type I adds two phosphates to serines at the end of the Smad tail. The receptor just signalled straight to a DNA-binding protein.

scenes.tts: Each phosphorylated tail fits a pocket on a neighbouring Smad. Typically, two phosphorylated Smads leave the receptor and join one shared partner, violet Smad four. This three-part complex accumulates in the nucleus to meet DNA. Meanwhile, active type one keeps phosphorylating more Smads until brakes intervene.
scenes.caption: Each phosphorylated tail fits a pocket on a neighbouring Smad. Typically, two phosphorylated Smads leave the receptor and join one shared partner, violet Smad4. This three-part complex accumulates in the nucleus to meet DNA. Meanwhile, active type I keeps phosphorylating more Smads until brakes intervene.
scenes.visual: Emerald phosphorylated R-Smad detaches as a second emerald R-Smad receives yellow phosphates from the active Type I kinase (showing catalytic turnover). Both emerald R-Smads snap tail-to-pocket with one violet block ('Smad4') into a compact three-part ring. The ring glides smoothly down-right across the glowing nuclear rim into the nucleus.
scenes.narration: Each phosphorylated tail fits a pocket on a neighbouring Smad. Typically, two phosphorylated Smads leave the receptor and join one shared partner, violet Smad4. This three-part complex accumulates in the nucleus to meet DNA. Meanwhile, active type I keeps phosphorylating more Smads until brakes intervene.

scenes.tts: The family splits into two branches built on one design. TGF beta and activin receptors phosphorylate emerald Smad two and Smad three. Bone morphogenetic protein, or BMP, receptors phosphorylate coral Smad one, five, and eight. Some BMPs grip type one tighter, yet phosphate still flows from type two, to type one, to the Smad.
scenes.caption: The family splits into two branches built on one design. TGF-β and activin receptors phosphorylate emerald Smad2 and Smad3. Bone morphogenetic protein, or BMP, receptors phosphorylate coral Smad1, 5, and 8. Some BMPs grip type I tighter, yet phosphate still flows from type II, to type I, to the Smad.
scenes.visual: Carried membrane splits cleanly into two parallel bays (schematic). Left bay: amber TGF-β/activin dimer on cyan Type II + indigo Type I passing yellow phosphate to emerald 'Smad2 / Smad3'. Right bay: coral BMP dimer gripping indigo Type I + cyan Type II, with yellow phosphate still arcing from cyan Type II to indigo Type I to coral 'Smad1 / Smad5 / Smad8'. Both branches funnel downward toward a shared violet 'Smad4' hub above the nuclear rim.
scenes.narration: The family splits into two branches built on one design. TGF-β and activin receptors phosphorylate emerald Smad2 and Smad3. Bone morphogenetic protein, or BMP, receptors phosphorylate coral Smad1, 5, and 8. Some BMPs grip type I tighter, yet phosphate still flows from type II, to type I, to the Smad.

scenes.tts: Notice the shared logic across both branches of the family. TGF beta is not an enzyme. It bridges always-active type two and locked type one, sending phosphate one way to a Smad. Next, see how that same Smad message gives opposite answers in different cells.
scenes.caption: Notice the shared logic across both branches of the family. TGF-β is not an enzyme. It bridges always-active type II and locked type I, sending phosphate one way to a Smad. Next, see how that same Smad message gives opposite answers in different cells.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls smoothly back to the unified single-membrane view as a clean yellow pulse travels once more along the live pathway: amber ligand bridges cyan Type II to indigo Type I → yellow P on GS domain → yellow P on emerald R-Smad → emerald/violet Smad4 trimer enters the glowing nucleus.
scenes.narration: Notice the shared logic across both branches of the family. TGF-β is not an enzyme. It bridges always-active type II and locked type I, sending phosphate one way to a Smad. Next, see how that same Smad message gives opposite answers in different cells.

scenes.visual: Clean dark navy end card with a subtle horizontal amber-to-emerald rule above a single centred line in crisp white type, nothing underneath: 'TGF-β bridges two kinases, passing phosphate one way to a Smad.'
